Limit
LIM-it
n. (a boundary; the utmost extent or point beyond which a thing does not or may not pass)
Latin limes, a boundary, a frontier, especially the fortified border of a Roman province. A limit is, at root, a marked edge, the line beyond which one territory ends and another begins.

Biblical Definition

Ezekiel's closing vision of the restored temple ends its detailed measurements with a single, sweeping statement of the whole complex's outer boundary: Upon the top of the mountain the whole limit thereof round about shall be most holy. After chapter upon chapter of exact cubits for gates, chambers, and courts, the vision steps back to name the one fact that governs every measurement already given — the entire enclosed limit, not merely the innermost sanctuary, is most holy ground, a single boundary drawn around the whole rather than a series of graduated zones of lesser and greater sanctity.

The verse's placement matters as much as its content. It comes immediately after the command that the house's whole form, fashion, goings out, comings in, and laws be written down and kept, so that a people ashamed of their former sins might return to a pattern they can actually see and follow. A limit given in such exact, recorded detail is not an arbitrary restriction; it is the visible edge of a holiness the LORD Himself is willing to specify to the last cubit, precisely so that no one inside it could plausibly claim ignorance of where the boundary lay. Scripture's holiness is not vague to Ezekiel's audience; it has a limit, and the limit is drawn and measured before a single stone is set in place.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): the utmost extent; the bound or boundary of a thing; the line or point beyond which a thing cannot or may not pass.

expand to see more

LIMIT, n. The bound or utmost extent of a thing; a boundary line, real or imaginary, beyond which extension does not take place.

HOLY, a. Set apart for sacred use; free from sin; consecrated to the service of God.

SANCTUARY, n. A sacred place; the most holy part of a temple; a place of protection.

MEASURE, v.t. To ascertain the dimensions, quantity, or extent of, by a fixed standard.

PATTERN, n. A model or original to be copied or imitated; a form or plan to be followed exactly.

Key Scripture

Eze 43:11 — "And if they be ashamed of all that they have done, shew them the form of the house, and the fashion thereof, and the goings out thereof, and the comings in thereof, and all the forms thereof, and all the ordinances thereof, and all the forms thereof, and all the laws thereof: and write it in their sight, that they may keep the whole form thereof, and all the ordinances thereof, and do them."

Eze 43:12 — "This is the law of the house; Upon the top of the mountain the whole limit thereof round about shall be most holy. Behold, this is the law of the house."

Eze 42:20 — "He measured it by the four sides: it had a wall round about, five hundred reeds long, and five hundred broad, to make a separation between the sanctuary and the profane place."

Lev 10:10 — "And that ye may put difference between holy and unholy, and between unclean and clean;"

Modern Corruption

A limit is treated as an arbitrary restriction imposed to constrain freedom, when Ezekiel's temple limit is given in exact, recorded measurement precisely so that holiness would be knowable and followable rather than left to guesswork.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; a limit still names a boundary. The principle worth recovering is why Ezekiel's vision bothers to measure the limit at all, down to the cubit, rather than simply declaring the temple holy in general terms. A limit that cannot be located is not a real limit; it is a vague warning that leaves everyone unsure how close they may safely come.

The command to write the whole pattern down, so that a people ashamed of their past sins could keep it, shows the limit functioning as mercy rather than mere restriction. Leviticus states the underlying principle plainly: putting a difference between holy and unholy is itself a duty, and a limit precisely drawn is how that difference becomes something ordinary people can actually recognize and honor, rather than a holiness so undefined it can only ever be transgressed by accident.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew gebul (H1366), a border, a boundary, a limit; the standing Old Testament word for territorial and sacred boundaries alike.

expand to see more

Hebrew gebul (H1366) — a border, boundary, limit; the noun rendered “limit” in Ezekiel 43:12, elsewhere used of tribal and national borders.

Hebrew qodesh (H6944) — holiness, a holy thing, a sacred place; the quality declared of the whole limit, most holy.

Hebrew tokniyth (H8508) — a measurement, a proportion, a pattern; the standing word for the exact form Ezekiel is shown throughout the temple vision.

Hebrew badal (H914) — to divide, to separate, to make a distinction; the verb behind Leviticus 10:10's command to put a difference between holy and unholy.

Hebrew bosh (H954, in the sense of shame) — to be ashamed; the condition of the people the whole vision's exact pattern is meant to address, Ezekiel 43:10-11.

Usage

"“the whole limit thereof round about shall be most holy” — the boundary of Ezekiel's temple vision."

"“write it in their sight, that they may keep the whole form thereof” — the exact pattern given so the limit could be known."

"“put difference between holy and unholy” — the underlying principle a measured limit serves."
